Calculate CD interest and maturity value

This certificate of deposit calculator estimates how a fixed deposit can grow over a stated term. Enter the opening deposit, choose whether the quoted rate is APY or a nominal annual rate, select the compounding frequency, and enter the term in years and months. The results show the projected maturity balance, total interest, effective annual yield, estimated after-tax earnings, and inflation-adjusted purchasing power.

The calculator assumes the rate remains fixed, interest stays in the CD and compounds, there are no additional deposits, and no money is withdrawn before the selected term ends. Actual bank disclosures control crediting, day-count, rounding, renewal, grace-period, and penalty rules.

CD maturity value formula

When the input is a nominal annual rate, the calculator divides that rate by the number of compounding periods per year and applies compound growth for the term.

maturity value = principal x (1 + annual rate / n)^(n x years)
total interest = maturity value - principal

Here, n is 365 for daily compounding, 12 for monthly, 4 for quarterly, 2 for semiannual, or 1 for annual. A partial-year term is represented by total months divided by 12. For example, $10,000 at a 5% nominal annual rate compounded monthly for three years grows to about $11,614.72 before tax.

APY versus nominal annual rate

Annual percentage yield, or APY, already reflects the effect of compounding over one year. If a bank advertises 5.00% APY, select APY and enter 5. The calculator applies an effective 5% annual growth rate; changing the compounding menu does not change the answer because the compounding effect is already embedded in APY.

A nominal annual rate does not include the full annual compounding effect. For that input, compounding frequency matters and the calculator derives APY:

APY = (1 + nominal annual rate / n)^n - 1

Do not enter an advertised APY as a nominal rate or the compounding effect will be counted twice. Compare offers using the rate label and assumptions shown in each institution's account disclosure.

CD calculation example

Suppose a CD starts with $10,000, earns 5.00% APY, and remains deposited for three years. Its projected maturity value is $10,000 x 1.05³, or $11,576.25. Total interest is $1,576.25. At an entered 24% marginal tax rate, a simplified estimate of tax on that interest is $378.30, leaving $1,197.95 of interest after the entered tax assumption.

This tax estimate does not determine when income is taxable, which rate applies, or whether deductions and account type change the result. It simply multiplies modeled interest by the rate entered.

Monthly and annual accumulation schedule

The result table provides a month-by-month balance and an annual summary. For consistent comparison across products, monthly rows use the effective monthly growth rate implied by the selected annual yield. A bank may credit interest daily, monthly, quarterly, at maturity, or on another schedule, so statement balances can differ slightly even when the disclosed APY is the same. The final modeled balance follows the selected APY or nominal-rate formula.

Estimated tax on CD interest

The IRS Publication 550 explains that interest from certificates of deposit and other deferred-interest accounts can be taxable and discusses when interest is included in income. It also explains reporting for penalties on early withdrawal. Tax timing can differ for a short-term CD, a CD with interest deferred for more than one year, a retirement account, and other arrangements.

The tax field is optional planning math, not tax advice. The calculator does not model federal brackets, state tax, original issue discount, tax-deferred accounts, tax forms, or the separate treatment of an early-withdrawal penalty. Enter zero when an after-tax estimate is not useful for the comparison.

Early withdrawal penalty estimate

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes a CD as a savings account in which money generally remains deposited for a specified period and notes that an early withdrawal usually means paying a penalty. Each institution sets its own terms.

Open the optional assumptions and enter the penalty as months of simple interest. This calculator estimates that amount from the initial principal and modeled effective annual yield, then subtracts it from the projected balance. It does not determine the bank's actual penalty, minimum penalty, principal invasion, partial-withdrawal rule, or the balance on a particular withdrawal date. Read the account agreement before acting.

Inflation-adjusted CD value

The real-value estimate divides the after-tax modeled maturity balance by compound inflation over the term. This expresses future dollars in approximate present purchasing power.

inflation-adjusted value = after-tax maturity value / (1 + inflation rate)^years

Inflation is uncertain, and the entered rate is not a forecast. Use it to compare scenarios rather than to predict exactly what goods and services will cost at maturity.

FDIC insurance and CD balances

Certificates of deposit are among the deposit products that can be insured when issued by an FDIC-insured bank. The FDIC's insured-products guidance explains that coverage depends on ownership category. The standard amount is $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each ownership category, and accounts in the same category at the same bank are generally combined for coverage purposes.

The calculator flags whether this single projected CD balance is above or below $250,000, but that is not an insurance determination. Other checking, savings, money market, and CD balances at the same bank can affect the total. Different ownership categories have detailed requirements. Use the FDIC's official tools or contact the institution to evaluate actual coverage. Credit union share insurance is administered separately by the NCUA.

How to compare CD offers

  • Compare APY using the same term length and deposit amount.
  • Check the minimum opening deposit and whether the quoted APY requires a particular balance.
  • Read the early-withdrawal penalty and whether it can reduce principal.
  • Confirm when interest is credited and whether it is automatically reinvested.
  • Review maturity notices, grace period, automatic renewal, and the renewal rate.
  • Consider whether liquidity matters more than a small yield difference.
  • Verify the issuing bank or credit union and applicable deposit insurance.

CD ladder planning

A CD ladder divides funds among CDs with different maturity dates. As each CD matures, the owner can use the cash or reinvest it at the long end of the ladder. This can create more frequent access than placing all funds in one long-term CD. A ladder does not guarantee better returns; future rates, penalties, reinvestment choices, and liquidity needs determine the outcome. Model each rung separately with the term and APY offered for that CD.

Frequently asked questions

How much will a $10,000 CD earn?

It depends on APY and term. At 5.00% APY for three years, the modeled maturity balance is $11,576.25 and total interest is $1,576.25 before tax.

Should I enter APY or interest rate?

Use the label in the bank's disclosure. Select APY when the quoted percentage is APY. Select nominal annual rate only when the quote excludes the annual compounding effect.

Does a CD compound daily or monthly?

Terms vary. Daily and monthly compounding are common, but the account disclosure controls. When APY is entered, the annual yield already incorporates compounding.

Is CD interest taxable?

CD interest is commonly taxable in the United States, but timing and treatment depend on the account and circumstances. Review current IRS guidance or consult a qualified tax professional.

Does this calculate an exact early withdrawal amount?

No. It provides a simple months-of-interest scenario. The issuing institution's agreement determines the actual penalty.
